---
title: "Molecular and Chemical Embeddings"
---

Small molecules are the other half of structural biology: drugs, metabolites,
cofactors, and substrates. Their representations share a problem with proteins —
the object is a graph, not a sequence — but the scales and constraints are
different. A molecule has tens of atoms, not hundreds of residues; it is
described by bonds and functional groups rather than a backbone; and its most
important question is usually quantitative, "what is the property or activity?",
rather than structural.

This chapter traces the path from hand-crafted chemical fingerprints to learned
molecular embeddings, and gives an explicit criterion for choosing between them
on a given quantitative structure–property or structure–activity relationship
(QSPR/QSAR) task.

# Classical Fingerprints and Descriptors

For decades, molecules have been encoded as fixed-length vectors by deterministic
rules. These encodings remain strong baselines and are still widely used.

## Extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFP/Morgan)

The extended-connectivity fingerprint (ECFP) [@rogers2010extended] is the
dominant topological fingerprint. Give each atom $i$ an initial invariant integer
label $\ell_i^{(0)}$ computed from local features (element, degree, charge,
attached hydrogens, ring membership), and propagate labels around each atom for
$R$ iterations,

$$ \ell_i^{(r+1)} = h\!\left(\ell_i^{(r)}, \left\{\ell_j^{(r)} : j \in \mathcal{N}(i)\right\}\right), \qquad r = 0, \dots, R - 1 $$ {#eq-ch07-ecfp-label}

where $\mathcal{N}(i)$ is the set of bonded neighbors of atom $i$ and $h$ is a
deterministic hash that treats its second argument as an *unordered* multiset, so
that the update does not depend on the order in which neighbors are listed. The
widely used Morgan algorithm is a specific implementation of this scheme. For a
molecule $M$, each identifier $(\ell_i^{(r)}, r)$ is then hashed into a fixed-length
bit vector
$\mathrm{ECFP}(M) \in \{0,1\}^{b}$ of length $b$ (commonly $1024$ or $2048$),

$$ \mathrm{ECFP}(M) = \bigvee_{i,\, r} e_{\,h'(\ell_i^{(r)},\, r)} $$ {#eq-ch07-ecfp}

where $h'$ maps an identifier to a bit index in $\{1, \dots, b\}$,
$e_k \in \{0,1\}^b$ is the $k$-th standard basis vector (a 1 in position $k$),
and $\bigvee$ is the bitwise OR over all identifiers.

Two properties follow directly from (@eq-ch07-ecfp). First, a molecule with
$n$ atoms generates at most $n(R+1)$ identifiers, so $\mathrm{ECFP}(M)$ has at
most $n(R+1)$ set bits out of $b$; because $n(R+1) \ll b$ in practice the vector
is **sparse and high-dimensional**. Second, because $h'$ maps an unbounded set of
identifiers into only $b$ bins, distinct substructures *collide* whenever
$h'(\ell, r) = h'(\ell', r')$; under a uniform hash the expected number of
colliding identifier pairs is approximately $\binom{m}{2}/b$ for $m$ identifiers
present, so increasing $b$ reduces collisions at linear memory cost while a small
$b$ trades accuracy for a compact, cache-friendly vector. The fingerprint length
is therefore a hyperparameter, not a consequence of chemistry: a collision is a
tolerable loss for similarity search but a source of noise when the vector is
used as a model input.

ECFP is invariant by construction to atom numbering (@eq-ch07-ecfp-label uses
unordered neighbor sets), and captures local substructure well, which is why it
is a fixture in similarity search and virtual screening. Because ECFP vectors are
binary and high-dimensional, they are compared with the Tanimoto coefficient
rather than Euclidean distance. For $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \{0,1\}^{b}$ the
Tanimoto coefficient is

$$ T(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}{\lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert_1 + \lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert_1 - \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle} \in [0, 1] $$ {#eq-ch07-tanimoto}

where $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$ counts shared set bits and
$\lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert_1 + \lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert_1 - \langle \mathbf{u},
\mathbf{v} \rangle$ counts the union of set bits; the coefficient $T$ of
(@eq-ch07-tanimoto) is thus the fraction of substructures present in either
molecule that are present in both, and a value near one indicates largely shared
substructure.

## MACCS keys

The MACCS keys [@durant2002reoptimization] are a complementary, much smaller
fingerprint: a fixed dictionary of a few hundred predefined substructural
queries, each answered present or absent. Because the bits have human-assigned
meanings, MACCS keys are more interpretable than hashed circular fingerprints,
at the cost of covering far fewer substructures.

## Physicochemical descriptors

A third classical family is not a fingerprint at all but a vector of global
physicochemical properties: molecular weight, lipophilicity (logP), polar surface
area, counts of hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, rotatable bonds, and so on.
These descriptors are continuous, low-dimensional, and directly meaningful, but
they discard most of the graph's topology.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
A **molecular fingerprint** is a fixed-length vector computed from a molecule by a
deterministic rule, with no parameters learned from data. A **learned molecular
embedding** is a vector produced by a model (graph neural network or language
model) whose parameters are optimized on a corpus of molecules and/or labels. The
distinction is *not* sparse-versus-dense; it is rule-based versus learned, which
drives everything about data requirements, transfer, and interpretability.
:::

# String-Based Learned Embeddings

## SMILES

Many molecular models never look at the graph directly. Instead they read the
molecule as a **SMILES** string, a linear textual encoding of the graph produced
by a deterministic traversal [@weininger1988smiles]. SMILES turns chemistry into a
language-modelling problem, letting sequence architectures be applied off the
shelf. Its weakness is that a single molecule has many equivalent SMILES
(different valid traversals), so the same graph maps to different strings; models
must be trained to be robust to this, for example by enumeration.

## Mol2Vec

Mol2Vec [@jaeger2018mol2vec] applies the word2vec idea [@mikolov2013efficient]
from Chapter 3 to chemistry: it treats substructures (Morgan-style atom
environments) as "words" and molecules as "sentences", and learns a dense vector
per substructure with skip-gram. A molecule embedding is then the sum of its substructure vectors. This
is an *unsupervised, string- and substructure-based* embedding that can be
computed without labels and used to warm-start property models.

## ChemBERTa

ChemBERTa [@chithrananda2020chemberta] is a transformer language model pretrained
on large libraries of SMILES with masked-language-modeling, then fine-tuned for
molecular property prediction. It demonstrated that standard masked pretraining
on SMILES yields competitive property predictors, and it set the template for the
many subsequent SMILES transformers.

## MolBERT

MolBERT [@fabian2020molbert] extends the pretraining recipe with
*domain-relevant auxiliary tasks* — for example predicting molecular descriptors
or graph-derived quantities alongside masked-token prediction — and with physical
augmentations of the input. The auxiliary objectives inject chemical inductive
bias that masked language modeling on SMILES alone lacks, improving robustness on
downstream property benchmarks.

# Graph Neural Networks for Molecules

Reading a molecule as a string is convenient but throws away the graph structure
and re-introduces the traversal-ambiguity problem. Graph neural networks operate
on the molecule graph directly; the full path from molecule to graph to embedding
is summarized in @fig-mol-graph.

## Message passing

The neural message-passing framework [@gilmer2017neural] defines a molecule as a
graph $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ with atom features and bond
features and computes each atom's embedding by iteratively aggregating messages
from its bonded neighbors. With $\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ the
embedding of atom $i$ at layer $l$, $\mathbf{e}_{ij} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_e}$ the
bond features of edge $(i, j)$, and $\mathcal{N}(i)$ the neighbor set,

$$ \mathbf{h}_i^{(l+1)} = U\!\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)},\ \bigoplus_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \mathrm{Msg}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)}, \mathbf{h}_j^{(l)}, \mathbf{e}_{ij}\right)\right) $$ {#eq-ch07-mpnn}

where $\mathrm{Msg}$ and $U$ are learned message and update functions and $\bigoplus$ is a
permutation-invariant aggregator (sum, mean, or max). After $L$ rounds of
(@eq-ch07-mpnn), a permutation-invariant readout collapses the atom
embeddings into one molecule vector $\mathbf{z}_M \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$,

$$ \mathbf{z}_M = R\!\left(\left\{\mathbf{h}_i^{(L)}\right\}_{i \in \mathcal{V}}\right), \qquad R\!\left(\left\{\mathbf{h}_{\pi(i)}\right\}_{i \in \mathcal{V}}\right) = R\!\left(\left\{\mathbf{h}_i\right\}_{i \in \mathcal{V}}\right) \ \ \text{for every permutation } \pi $$ {#eq-ch07-mol-readout}

where $L$ is the number of layers and $R$ is sum, mean, or attention pooling.
Because both $\bigoplus$ and $R$ are permutation-invariant, the molecule
embedding does not depend on the arbitrary atom indexing used to build the graph
— the molecular analogue of the residue-order independence of Chapter 6.

## D-MPNN and Chemprop

The directed message-passing neural network (D-MPNN) used by Chemprop
[@yang2019analyzing] sends messages along *directed edges* rather than at atoms.
Associate a hidden state $\mathbf{m}_{ij}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ with the
directed edge $i \to j$, initialized from atom and bond features as
$\mathbf{m}_{ij}^{(0)} = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i [\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{e}_{ij}])$,
and update it from the directed edges entering $i$ other than its reverse,

$$ \mathbf{m}_{ij}^{(l+1)} = U\!\left(\mathbf{m}_{ij}^{(0)},\ \bigoplus_{k \in \mathcal{N}(i) \setminus \{j\}} \mathrm{Msg}\!\left(\mathbf{m}_{ki}^{(l)}\right)\right) $$ {#eq-ch07-dmpnn}

and read out an atom embedding by pooling its incoming directed edges,
$\mathbf{h}_j = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o [\mathbf{x}_j, \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}(j)}
\mathbf{m}_{ij}^{(L)}])$. The exclusion $k \neq j$ in (@eq-ch07-dmpnn)
removes the reverse edge $j \to i$ from the aggregation, so a message cannot be
echoed straight back along the bond it arrived on; this refinement reduces
redundant propagation and is why D-MPNN became a standard baseline. Chemprop
showed that a carefully tuned D-MPNN matches or exceeds prior learned and
fingerprint-based models on many QSPR benchmarks, although the size of the
advantage depends on the dataset and target [@yang2019analyzing]; it is a
standard baseline for molecular property prediction.

## GIN

The graph isomorphism network (GIN) [@xu2019powerful] is notable for its
*theoretical* grounding: with an injective aggregation function and sufficient
depth, it is as discriminative as the Weisfeiler–Lehman graph-isomorphism test.
This makes GIN a principled choice when distinguishing similar substructures
matters, and it is a common backbone in molecular benchmarks.

## AttentiveFP

AttentiveFP [@xiong2020pushing] adds a graph attention mechanism with both atom-
and bond-level attention, allowing the model to weight the neighbors that matter
for a property rather than pooling them uniformly. Attention weights also provide
a crude form of interpretability, in that they can be inspected for
chemically salient substructures (with the usual caveats about attention as
explanation; see Chapter 12).

# Pretraining Strategies for Molecular Language Models

Learned molecular embeddings are only as good as their pretraining. Three ideas
recur.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Masked atom modeling** is the molecular analogue of masked-token pretraining:
a fraction of atoms (and/or bonds, or SMILES tokens) is hidden and the model must
reconstruct them from context. Because the reconstruction target encodes local
chemistry, the resulting embeddings encode functional-group and scaffold
regularity without any labeled property.
:::

First, **masked atom or masked token modeling**, as in ChemBERTa
[@chithrananda2020chemberta], learns from unlabeled molecule libraries at scale.
Second, **auxiliary self-supervised tasks** — predicting distances, bond
properties, or global descriptors — supply the chemical inductive bias that pure
masked modeling lacks, an approach formalized by MolBERT [@fabian2020molbert] and
central to structure-aware pretraining. Third, **contrastive learning**
[@chen2020simple], where two augmented views of the same molecule are pulled
together and different molecules pushed apart, is used to pretrain encoders that
transfer without labels. In all three cases the pretrained representation is
evaluated by linear probing or fine-tuning, exactly as for sequence models
(Chapter 5).

# Conformers and 3D-Aware Models

A molecule is a 3D object, and many properties — reactivity, binding, and
especially quantum-chemical targets — depend on geometry, not just connectivity.
A **conformer** is one 3D arrangement of the atoms; a molecule may have many.

## SchNet and DimeNet

SchNet [@schutt2017schnet] introduced continuous-filter convolutions over atom
positions, making the model sensitive to interatomic distances while remaining
invariant to rotation and translation. DimeNet [@gasteiger2020dimenet] added
*directional* messages: instead of using distances alone, it encodes angles
between bonds, which resolves configurations that distance-only models conflate.

## GemNet

GemNet [@gasteiger2021gemnet] generalizes directional message passing to
two-hop interactions and four-body (dihedral) terms, so that the representation
depends on the relative orientation of two bonds, not just their lengths and
angles. This is the geometry needed for accurate molecular simulation and
reaction modelling.

## Uni-Mol

Uni-Mol [@zhou2023unimol] is a pretrained, 3D-aware molecular representation: it
consumes atoms with coordinates and learns both atom-level and pair-level
embeddings, pretrained with masked-atom and coordinate-denoising objectives on
large conformer datasets. It shows that a single pretrained 3D encoder transfers
across property, docking, and conformer-generation tasks, the molecular
counterpart of a structure-based foundation model (Chapter 13).

These 3D models share one invariance. Their features are functions of pairwise
distances $\lVert \mathbf{x}_a - \mathbf{x}_b \rVert_2$, bond angles, and
dihedrals, all of which are invariant under a rigid motion, so a global rotation
$\mathbf{x}_a \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_a + \mathbf{t}$ (with
$\mathbf{R} \in SO(3)$, $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3$) leaves the learned
per-atom and per-molecule representations unchanged. The graph-only models of the
previous section are invariant to *permutation* by (@eq-ch07-mol-readout) but
blind to geometry; the 3D models replace the explicit bond graph with
geometry-derived features and so add E(3)-invariance of the conformation to the
permutation invariance they already have.

# Property and Activity Prediction

The practically important output of all this machinery is a molecule embedding
that feeds a downstream head for a task: predicting a continuous property
(logP, solubility, toxicity) is **QSPR**; predicting a biological activity or
binding label is **QSAR**. Formally, a molecular encoder $\mathrm{Enc}_\theta$
maps a molecule $M$ to an embedding
$\mathbf{z}_M = \mathrm{Enc}_\theta(M) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, and a prediction head
$g_\phi$ is fit together with the encoder by minimizing an empirical risk over a
labeled dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(M, y_M)\}$,

$$ \min_{\theta, \phi}\ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|} \sum_{(M, y_M) \in \mathcal{D}} \ell\!\left(g_\phi(\mathbf{z}_M),\ y_M\right) $$ {#eq-ch07-mol-prediction}

where $\ell$ is the loss and the minimization is over the encoder parameters
$\theta$ and head parameters $\phi$. For a continuous property (QSPR), $\ell$ is
the squared error $\lVert g_\phi(\mathbf{z}_M) - y_M \rVert_2^2$; for a binary
activity label (QSAR), it is the cross-entropy
$-[y_M \log \hat{y}_M + (1 - y_M)\log(1 - \hat{y}_M)]$ with
$\hat{y}_M = \operatorname{sigmoid}(g_\phi(\mathbf{z}_M))$. For a classical
fingerprint the encoder has no learned parameters ($\theta = \varnothing$) and
only the head is trained, which is why fingerprints are usable in the low-data
regime; for a learned encoder the gradient also updates $\theta$ in
(@eq-ch07-mol-prediction), which is what makes pretraining transferable but raises the
data requirement. The recurring empirical findings are:

- On small, homogeneous, well-split datasets, classical fingerprints combined
  with gradient-boosted trees or random forests remain extremely competitive, and
  are far cheaper [@rogers2010extended; @yang2019analyzing].
- Learned graph and SMILES embeddings win when data are plentiful or when
  pretraining transfers from related tasks, and when the target depends on
  geometry rather than 2D topology [@yang2019analyzing; @zhou2023unimol].
- The split matters more than the model. Random splits can substantially
  overstate performance relative to *scaffold* splits, which hold out whole
  chemical scaffolds [@bemis1996properties; @chuang2018adversarial]; the leakage
  pitfalls of Chapter 11 apply with particular force here.

In practice a molecule is rarely predicted once. Modern pipelines attach several
heads to a shared embedding (multi-task learning), which shares statistical
strength across related endpoints and is a central draw of a learned
representation: one embedding can serve logP, solubility, and activity models at
once. Learned embeddings also admit uncertainty estimates, through ensembling or
a probabilistic head, whereas a fingerprint gives no such signal. The practical
recommendation is therefore not "learned always wins" but a decision governed by
data volume, the relevance of 3D geometry to the target, and whether the same
molecule must serve many endpoints.

@tbl-fingerprint-learned summarizes the trade-offs that determine the
choice.

| Criterion | Classical fingerprints / descriptors | Learned embeddings |
|:--|:--|:--|
| How computed | deterministic rule, no training | trained GNN or language model |
| Dimensionality | fixed, often sparse (hundreds–thousands of bits) | dense, typically 64–1024 |
| Data required | works with very few labels | benefits from large pretraining corpora |
| Transfer to new tasks | weak; recompute per task | strong with pretraining + fine-tuning |
| Uses 3D geometry | no (2D topology) | yes for conformer-aware models |
| Interpretability | substructure bits largely human-readable | low; requires probing |
| Compute cost | negligible | training/inference cost |
| Typical strength | similarity search, low-data baselines | large-data QSPR/QSAR, 3D-dependent targets |

: Fingerprints versus learned embeddings. The choice is governed by data volume,
whether 3D geometry matters, and how much interpretability is required — not by
which method is newer. {#tbl-fingerprint-learned}

::: {#fig-mol-graph}
```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["SMILES / 2D depiction"] --> B["Atoms + bonds"]
  B --> C["Molecule graph<br/>node features: element, charge, degree, ring<br/>edge features: bond order, ring, stereo"]
  C --> D["GNN message passing<br/>(L layers, e.g. MPNN, D-MPNN, GIN)"]
  D --> E["Atom embeddings"]
  E --> F["Readout / pooling<br/>(sum, mean, attention)"]
  F --> G["Molecule embedding"]
  G --> H["Property head<br/>(QSPR / QSAR)"]
  C -.->|"3D conformer (optional)"| D
```

From molecule to graph to embedding. A molecular structure is parsed into a graph with atom and bond features; a message-passing network produces per-atom embeddings, which a permutation-invariant readout pools into a single molecule vector used by a property head. The dashed path shows optional 3D conformer information feeding the network, as in SchNet, DimeNet, GemNet, and Uni-Mol.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaways
- Fingerprints such as ECFP [@rogers2010extended] and MACCS
  [@durant2002reoptimization] are deterministic, need no training, and remain
  strong low-data and similarity-search baselines; learned embeddings win when
  data or geometry demand it.
- SMILES [@weininger1988smiles] turns chemistry into a language task, enabling
  word2vec-style and transformer methods (Mol2Vec [@jaeger2018mol2vec],
  ChemBERTa [@chithrananda2020chemberta], MolBERT [@fabian2020molbert]), at the
  cost of traversal ambiguity.
- Message-passing GNNs operate on the graph directly: MPNN [@gilmer2017neural]
  sets the framework, D-MPNN/Chemprop [@yang2019analyzing] is the standard
  baseline, GIN [@xu2019powerful] adds expressiveness guarantees, and AttentiveFP
  [@xiong2020pushing] adds attention.
- Pretraining (masked atom modeling, auxiliary tasks, contrastive objectives)
  is what makes learned molecular embeddings transfer; without it, fingerprints
  are often preferable.
- 3D-aware models — SchNet [@schutt2017schnet], DimeNet [@gasteiger2020dimenet],
  GemNet [@gasteiger2021gemnet], Uni-Mol [@zhou2023unimol] — are required when
  the target depends on conformation rather than 2D topology.
- Splitting strategy, not architecture, is the dominant source of error in
  QSPR/QSAR; use scaffold splits (Chapter 11).
:::
